bottleneck: Optogenetics gives cell-type-specific control of neurons with light, but translating it to humans requires gene therapy to express opsins plus implanted light sources — combining the risks of both modalities in one intervention. Light scatters in brain tissue, limiting effective depth to millimeters, and the safety of chronic opsin expression in human neurons over decades is entirely unproven. The most precise neural control tool in neuroscience cannot reach the clinic it was built for, leaving human neuromodulation stuck with the blunt electricity of DBS while mice enjoy single-cell-type precision.
current_state: Optogenetics is routine in animals and in early human retinal trials, where light delivery is natural, but deep-brain therapeutic use remains preclinical with no clinical path.
title: Optogenetics cannot reach human therapy
why_it_blocks: Cell-type-specific control would revolutionize psychiatry and neurology — treating depression by modulating one cell type, not bathing regions in current. But the delivery chain (genes plus light plus lifetime safety) has no viable human configuration yet.
